title: Power Shift: Renewables and the Grid

transcript.speaker: Elena
transcript.text: Welcome to Climate Desk. I'm Elena Rossi, and today I'm talking energy transition with climate scientist Dr. Sam Okafor.

transcript.speaker: Sam
transcript.text: Thanks Elena, glad to be here.

transcript.speaker: Elena
transcript.text: Let's start with temperature. How bad was last year?

transcript.speaker: Sam
transcript.text: 2024 was the hottest year on record, and the first calendar year where the global average went more than 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels.

transcript.speaker: Elena
transcript.text: Does that mean the Paris goals are dead?

transcript.speaker: Sam
transcript.text: I'd call it a warning shot, not a death certificate. But it should scare policymakers.

transcript.speaker: Elena
transcript.text: On the clean energy side, I feel like renewables are still a rounding error. They're under 20% of the world's electricity.

transcript.speaker: Sam
transcript.text: I hear that all the time, and I think the growth curve is the story people keep missing.

transcript.speaker: Sam
transcript.text: China, by a mile. China installed more than half of all the new solar capacity in the world in 2023.

transcript.speaker: Elena
transcript.text: And where are carbon dioxide levels these days?

transcript.speaker: Sam
transcript.text: We're at around 350 parts per million of CO2 in the atmosphere, which is the level scientists were warning about decades ago.

transcript.speaker: Elena
transcript.text: Is anything working at the local level?

transcript.speaker: Sam
transcript.text: At our institute we put solar panels on the roof two years ago and our electric bill dropped about 40%.

transcript.speaker: Sam
transcript.text: Commercial fusion plants will be supplying power to the grid by 2035.

transcript.speaker: Elena
transcript.text: We'll hold you to that. Sam Okafor, thanks for joining Climate Desk.
